text: Service request management exists to support the agreed quality of a service by handling predefined, user-initiated service requests in an effective, user-friendly way. Nothing is broken here — the service already works exactly as designed, and the user just needs the provider to do one of the things it's built to do.

That's the clean line against incident management, which you covered back in chapter four. An incident is an unplanned interruption or a reduction in quality — something is wrong. A service request is a planned, expected, routine ask: a new laptop, access to a shared drive, a password reset, a how-do-I question answered. Same ticket queue, very different kind of work.

The word predefined is doing real work in that purpose statement. ITIL 4 doesn't picture this practice improvising a process for every ticket. Requests are thought through in advance: what information is needed, who has to approve it, what steps fulfill it, and roughly how long it should take. Standardizing ahead of time is what makes the practice fast and consistent instead of reinventing the wheel.

The usual mechanism for surfacing those predefined requests is a service catalog, sometimes called a request catalog — a menu of exactly what can be asked for, with the needed information captured up front. Clicking request new laptop pulls in the model, the cost center, and the approver in one step, instead of a vague email someone has to interpret later.

Many catalog requests carry a built-in approval step — a manager signing off on a purchase, security approving elevated access — designed into the workflow itself, not handled as a side conversation. Other requests, like a password reset or a simple information request, skip approval and fulfill automatically, because the risk was already judged low enough when the request was designed.

Predefined, cataloged, and either approved or pre-approved by design — that's service request management in one line. Next up: knowledge management, where the organization turns what it's already learned into faster resolutions for everyone else.
